query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior under demanding service arises when high strain rate and moderate to elevated service temperatures dynamically refine the grain size below a critical threshold. This extreme grain refinement suppresses dislocation‐mediated plasticity and shifts deformation to grain-boundary–dominated processes, which in turn promote localized decohesion (or cavitation) along high-angle boundaries even in the absence of significant impurity segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a coarse or moderately sized grain structure (e.g., as typically produced by additive manufacturing) and negligible grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical deformation under varying strain rates combined with moderate to elevated temperatures, designed to induce dynamic shear and corresponding grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Compare tests under low-strain-rate and lower temperature conditions (baseline) with tests at higher strain rates and intermediate temperatures (e.g., 400–800°C) that are known to promote severe plastic deformation and dynamic grain refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic grain refinement leading to a nano-grained (or even locally amorphous) structure at the grain boundaries, resulting in a critical reduction of grain size and altered boundary cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At high strain rates and moderate temperatures, the severe plastic deformation leads to an inverse Hall-Petch effect whereby dislocation activity is suppressed and grain-boundary sliding becomes dominant. This induces localized decohesion (cavitation) at high-angle grain boundaries, precipitating brittle failure even though the alloy remains a solid solution without the conventional segregation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the high strain rate and intermediate temperature conditions, the alloy should exhibit reduced ductility, premature fracture initiating along refined grain boundaries, and increased signatures of brittle decohesion compared to the baseline state, where dislocation slip and conventional plastic flow dominate.
generation.baseline: Under lower strain rate and/or lower temperature conditions, the alloy maintains a coarser grain structure where conventional dislocation-mediated plasticity ensures higher ductility and toughness without immediate brittle failure.
generation.boundary: This brittle behavior is expected only within a service window where the applied strain rate and temperature are sufficiently high to induce extreme grain refinement (below a critical nanometer-scale grain size) but not so high as to trigger other degradation mechanisms like oxidation or phase transformation that complicate the analysis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical grain size and temperature/strain-rate thresholds where the transition from ductile to brittle behavior occurs are not well established and likely depend on the alloy’s detailed composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the targeted high-entropy alloy in the as-manufactured single-phase state. Perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or sliding wear tests) under two sets of conditions: (1) low strain rate and low to moderate temperature (baseline) and (2) high strain rate combined with intermediate temperatures (400–800°C). Use in-situ or post-mortem high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM, SEM) to characterize the grain structure (grain size, evidence of dynamic amorphization) and inspect fracture surfaces to determine whether failure initiates along refined grain boundaries.
measurements: Grain size distributions (via TEM/SEM) before and after deformation
Mechanical property metrics (ductility, fracture toughness, yield strength)
Fractography to identify signs of intergranular decohesion or cavitation
In-situ monitoring of surface shear strength or friction coefficients during sliding tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high strain rate and elevated temperature condition does not result in significant dynamic grain refinement (i.e., no reduction to the critical nanometer-scale grain size) or if brittle intergranular failure is not observed—instead the material maintains ductile behavior equivalent to the baseline—then the hypothesis that dynamic grain refinement triggers brittle behavior via grain-boundary decohesion is falsified.

Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
